# Formatting conversations for training {#sec-formatting} **You will learn:** - how a ConvFinQA conversation becomes one training sequence, and exactly which tokens the loss counts; - why one sequence per conversation is as good as one per turn; - how training, validation and dev data are kept apart, and how the prompt for each turn is built when we evaluate. @sec-base-instruct explained chat templates and teacher forcing in general. This chapter fixes the format we use for ConvFinQA, shows it on a real conversation, and checks the properties the later chapters rely on. Nothing here trains a model: it prepares the data that the training and evaluation chapters read. ## The messages A conversation becomes one chat. A fixed system message comes first. The first user message holds the page, that is the text before the table, the table as markdown and the text after it, followed by the first question. The assistant's reply is the gold program for that turn. Each later turn adds a user message with the question alone, and the assistant's reply with its gold program. `formatting.conversation_messages` does this. Here it is on a validation conversation with three turns: ::: {#f7a9ca3a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from IPython.display import HTML, display from convfinqa import data from convfinqa.artifacts import get from convfinqa.formatting import conversation_messages val = list(get("train_val_split").jsonl("val.jsonl")) three = [c for c in val if len(c["annotation"]["turn_program"]) == 3] conv = min( three, key=lambda c: sum(len(p) for p in c["annotation"]["turn_program"]) ) messages = conversation_messages(conv) def short(text, head=110, tail=60): text = text.replace("\n", " ⏎ ") return ( text if len(text) <= head + tail + 5 else text[:head] + " … " + text[-tail:] ) print(conv["id"], f"(Type {data.conversation_type(conv)})\n") for m in messages: print(f"{m['role']:>9}: {short(m['content'])}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Double_ADBE/2003/page_90.pdf (Type II) system: Answer with a program in the ConvFinQA DSL. user: building . the construction of the building was completed in december 2003 . due to lower than expected financ … ating leases net of sublease income due in less than 1 year? assistant: 23.6 user: what about the total non-cancelable operating leases net of sublease income? assistant: 83.9 user: what portion is due in less than 1 year? assistant: divide(23.6, 83.9) ``` ::: ::: The page appears once, in the first user message, because it does not change. The later questions refer to it and to the earlier answers, as a real conversation would. ## What the loss counts The messages are turned into token ids by the model's chat template, and a second list, the `labels`, says which of those tokens the model is trained to produce. A label is the token id where the token counts and `-100` where it does not (@sec-fine-tuning showed why the value is `-100`). The rule is simple: **only the assistant's answers count**, together with the `<|im_end|>` token that ends each one. @fig-sequence-layout shows the layout. ![Two ways to lay out the training data for a conversation of three turns (not to scale: the page is the long part). One sequence per conversation reads the page once and trains all three answers. One sequence per turn trains the same three answers, but reads the page and the earlier answers again for every turn.](figures/sequence_layout.svg){#fig-sequence-layout fig-alt="Two groups of bars. The first group has one bar: a system box, a long page-and-first-question box, then answer 1, question 2, answer 2, question 3 and answer 3, with the three answers in green. The second group has three bars, for turns 1, 2 and 3. Each starts with the same system and page boxes and ends with its own answer in green, and the earlier answers and questions are grey, so the page is repeated three times."} On our conversation, with the first part of the sequence cut off, the tokens look like this. Green tokens are trained, grey ones are only read: ::: {#c2a12807 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from transformers import AutoTokenizer from convfinqa.book.viz import trained_html from convfinqa.formatting import tokenize_conversation tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507") ids, labels = tokenize_conversation(tok, messages) first = next(i for i, label in enumerate(labels) if label != -100) start = first - 40 # the end of the first user message, and everything after it pieces = [tok.decode([i]) for i in ids[start:]] display(HTML( '
… (the first ' + f"{start:,}" + " tokens: the system message and the page)
" + trained_html(pieces, [label != -100 for label in labels[start:]]) )) print( f"{len(ids):,} tokens in all, " f"{sum(label != -100 for label in labels)} of them trained" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
… (the first 2,070 tokens: the system message and the page)
excess of applicable insurance coverage is minimal. .↵ ↵ Question: what is the amount of non-cancelable operating leases net of sublease income due in less than 1 year?<|im_end|>↵ <|im_start|>assistant↵ 23.6<|im_end|>↵ <|im_start|>user↵ what about the total non-cancelable operating leases net of sublease income?<|im_end|>↵ <|im_start|>assistant↵ 83.9<|im_end|>↵ <|im_start|>user↵ what portion is due in less than 1 year?<|im_end|>↵ <|im_start|>assistant↵ divide(23.6, 83.9)<|im_end|>↵
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2,179 tokens in all, 24 of them trained ``` ::: ::: How much of a sequence is trained? We can count over the whole validation split, and check that the count is the one the untuned model's loss was measured on in @sec-probing: ::: {#0af0d22e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print( "the template has generation markers:", "{% generation %}" in tok.chat_template ) total = trained = 0 for c in val: ids_c, labels_c = tokenize_conversation(tok, conversation_messages(c)) total += len(ids_c) trained += sum(label != -100 for label in labels_c) share = trained / total print(f"validation split: {total:,} tokens, {trained:,} trained ({share:.1%})") # the count the untuned loss was measured on assert trained == get("val_gold_nll").json("nll.json")["tokens"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` the template has generation markers: False validation split: 347,006 tokens, 16,417 trained (4.7%) ``` ::: ::: Three details of the layout: - **The answers are green, the markers around them are not.** The model is *given* `<|im_start|>assistant` and the newline that follows it, so these are grey: they are the generation prompt of the next section. It is asked to produce the answer and the `<|im_end|>` after it, which is how it learns to stop. The newline that the template writes after `<|im_end|>` is grey too. - **Most of the sequence is not trained.** The page and the questions are many tokens, and the answers few. Over the whole validation split the answers are 4\.7% of the tokens. - **The labels are ours.** The chat template of this model has no `{% generation %}` markers, which is what TRL's `assistant_only_loss` option needs. We do not need them: `tokenize_conversation` renders the chat up to each assistant message and finds the answer's tokens itself, and the Trainer uses a `labels` column as it is. ## One sequence per conversation Why is it allowed to train on all the answers of a conversation in one pass? Because the model is **causal**: the output at a position depends only on the tokens before it. The loss on the answer of turn $k$ therefore depends only on the tokens up to that answer, exactly as if the sequence had ended there. The summed loss of the whole conversation is the sum of the losses of the truncated sequences, and so is its gradient. `tests/test_causal_prefix.py` checks both on a small Qwen3, and also checks the limit of the claim: only the *end* of a conversation can be cut, because removing early tokens changes every later loss. Two training runs, one in each layout, are therefore equivalent up to batching (a step of 16 conversations holds far more answer tokens than a step of 16 turns) and rounding (different padding and batching change bf16 results), but not step for step. The saving is the one counted in @sec-base-instruct: the per-turn layout of @fig-sequence-layout reads several times as many tokens for the same answers. The price is the one named there too, **exposure bias**: during training every earlier answer in the context is the gold one. ::: {#920f99ec .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json from pathlib import Path lengths = json.loads(Path("../artifacts/processed/lengths.json").read_text()) assert lengths["longest"] <= lengths["max_length"] ``` ::: Nothing is cut by `max_length`: the longest full conversation of the data is 3\,460 tokens (@sec-convfinqa) and `max_length` is 3\,584. ## Train, validation and dev `train.json` is the training file. We hold out a tenth of its conversations as **[validation](901_glossary.qmd#gloss-validation)** data, for the choices that the project makes (the prompt, the checkpoint, the grammar) and train on the rest. Several conversations are written from the same report page, so the split is made **by page**: the group key is the conversation id without its `Single_` or `Double_` prefix and its `-N` suffix. A page then lies entirely on one side, and the model is never scored on a page it trained on. ::: {#6d308624 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd fit = list(get("train_val_split").jsonl("train_fit.jsonl")) dev = data.load_split("dev") print(conv["id"], "->", data.page_group(conv["id"])) pages = lambda convs: {data.page_group(c["id"]) for c in convs} n_turns = lambda convs: sum(len(c["annotation"]["dialogue_break"]) for c in convs) sizes = pd.DataFrame({ "conversations": { "train-fit": len(fit), "val": len(val), "dev": len(dev) }, "turns": { "train-fit": n_turns(fit), "val": n_turns(val), "dev": n_turns(dev) }, "pages": { "train-fit": len(pages(fit)), "val": len(pages(val)), "dev": len(pages(dev)) }, }) display(sizes) assert not pages(fit) & pages(val) print( f"dev pages that also occur in train: " f"{len(pages(dev) & (pages(fit) | pages(val)))} of {len(pages(dev))}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Double_ADBE/2003/page_90.pdf -> ADBE/2003/page_90.pdf ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
conversations turns pages
train-fit 2731 9979 1429
val 306 1125 159
dev 421 1490 218
``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dev pages that also occur in train: 0 of 218 ``` ::: ::: Train-fit and val together are 3\,037 conversations, the whole of `train.json`. The split is made once, with a fixed seed, and saved as the artifact `train_val_split`. **Dev is never used to make a choice.** The one use that the plan allows before the final evaluations is the one above: the page identifiers of dev are compared with train's, and no dev page is in train. That makes the validation data, which is disjoint from the training data by page, a fair stand-in for dev. The official test split has no labels and is not used. ## Prompts for evaluation At evaluation time the model sees the conversation up to the question of turn $k$, and writes the answer. The prompt is the training sequence cut right before that answer, with the generation prompt at the end. `formatting.prompt_messages` builds the chat. Earlier answers are the gold programs by default (the *gold history* of the evaluation chapters). The model's own earlier answers can be passed instead (the *predicted history*), and complete example conversations can be put in front (few-shot): ::: {#7e600338 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from convfinqa.formatting import prompt_messages def outline(chat): return " | ".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content'][:24]}…" for m in chat) print("gold history, turn 3:\n ", outline(prompt_messages(conv, 2)), "\n") print( "predicted history, turn 3:\n ", outline(prompt_messages( conv, 2, history=["(the model's answer 1)", "(the model's answer 2)"] )), "\n" ) print( "one example first, turn 3 (s = system, u = user, a = assistant):\n ", " ".join(m["role"][0] for m in prompt_messages(conv, 2, examples=[fit[0]])) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gold history, turn 3: system: Answer with a program in… | user: building . the construct… | assistant: 23.6… | user: what about the total non… | assistant: 83.9… | user: what portion is due in l… predicted history, turn 3: system: Answer with a program in… | user: building . the construct… | assistant: (the model's answer 1)… | user: what about the total non… | assistant: (the model's answer 2)… | user: what portion is due in l… one example first, turn 3 (s = system, u = user, a = assistant): s u a u a u a u a u a u a u ``` ::: ::: What the model reads in training and in evaluation must be the same, token for token, or the evaluation measures a different task from the one trained. We can check it on every turn of the validation split: the tokens of the prompt for turn $k$ must be the training sequence up to where the answer of turn $k$ begins. ::: {#80aa5d35 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def answer_starts(labels): return [ i for i, label in enumerate(labels) if label != -100 and (i == 0 or labels[i - 1] == -100) ] checked = 0 for c in val: ids_c, labels_c = tokenize_conversation(tok, conversation_messages(c)) starts = answer_starts(labels_c) assert len(starts) == len(data.turns(c)) for k, s in enumerate(starts): prompt = tok.apply_chat_template( prompt_messages(c, k), tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True ) assert tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"] == ids_c[:s] checked += 1 print( f"{checked:,} prompts checked: each is the training sequence up to the " "start of its answer" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1,125 prompts checked: each is the training sequence up to the start of its answer ``` ::: ::: ## The turns as tables For scoring, the evaluation chapters need the gold answer of every turn, and breakdowns by turn index and by conversation type. The artifact `eval_turns` holds them as one row per turn, for validation and for dev: ::: {#3acf48d4 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} tables = get("eval_turns") val_turns = pd.DataFrame(tables.jsonl("val_turns.jsonl")) dev_turns = pd.DataFrame(tables.jsonl("dev_turns.jsonl")) assert len(val_turns) == n_turns(val) and len(dev_turns) == n_turns(dev) == 1490 val_turns.head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
id turn n_turns question program answer part type number_turn
0 Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3 0 4 what is the net cash from operating activities... 206588 206588.0 0 I True
1 Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3 1 4 what about in 2008? 181001 181001.0 0 I True
2 Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3 2 4 what is the difference? subtract(206588, 181001) 25587.0 0 I False
3 Single_JKHY/2009/page_28.pdf-3 3 4 what percentage change does this represent? subtract(206588, 181001), divide(#0, 181001) 0.14136 0 I False
``` ::: ::: ::: {#30baaf14 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} longest = int(max(t["turn"].max() for t in (val_turns, dev_turns))) + 1 breakdown = { name: pd.crosstab(t["turn"] + 1, t["type"]).rename_axis("turn")\ .reindex(range(1, longest + 1), fill_value=0) for name, t in (("val", val_turns), ("dev", dev_turns)) } display(pd.concat(breakdown, axis=1)) print( "share of number-selection turns:", { name: f"{t.number_turn.mean():.0%}" for name, t in (("val", val_turns), ("dev", dev_turns)) } ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The evaluation chapters report accuracy by turn index and by conversation type, and these counts say how many turns each figure rests on. The program is written in the DSL throughout this chapter. Writing it as Python code instead, a later experiment of the book, changes the assistant's messages and nothing else here. ::: {.callout-tip title="Further reading"} - ConvFinQA's own files [@chen2022convfinqa] come in the same two shapes: whole conversations, and one row per turn, which is the per-turn layout of @fig-sequence-layout. :::
